title: El hecho de que + subjuntivo: nominalizar una idea

sections.content: El hecho de que + subjunctive turns a whole idea into the grammatical subject of a sentence -- "the fact that X" -- letting you evaluate or explain a situation rather than simply state it. Spanish defaults to the subjunctive here even when the fact is true, because the focus is on the fact's significance, not on asserting it. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: El hecho de que Madero no atendiera con suficiente urgencia la reforma agraria explica la ruptura casi inmediata con Zapata.
items.english: The fact that Madero did not address land reform with sufficient urgency explains the almost immediate break with Zapata.

items.spanish: El hecho de que Zapata y Villa tuvieran objetivos y estilos tan distintos no impidió que, en 1914, ambos ejércitos ocuparan juntos la Ciudad de México.
items.english: The fact that Zapata and Villa had such different goals and styles didn't prevent both armies from jointly occupying Mexico City in 1914.

items.spanish: El hecho de que esta alianza careciera de un programa político unificado explica por qué resultó tan efímera.
items.english: The fact that this alliance lacked a unified political program explains why it turned out so short-lived.

items.spanish: Tanto Zapata como Villa acabarían siendo asesinados, sin haber logrado nunca imponer plenamente su visión particular de la revolución.
items.english: Both Zapata and Villa would end up assassinated, having never managed to fully impose their particular vision of the revolution.

sections.content: El hecho de que always takes the subjunctive in careful written Spanish, unlike English "the fact that," which stays neutral about mood -- don't let the English translation pull you toward the indicative here.
